ENGINEERING - CAREER GUIDE

## Mechanical Engineer
Mechanical Engineers design, analyze, and test mechanical systems and
products - anything from vehicle components to manufacturing equipment.
Core skills: CAD software (SolidWorks, CATIA, AutoCAD), understanding of
materials and manufacturing processes, simulation/analysis tools (ANSYS,
FEA), and strong fundamentals in physics and thermodynamics.
Common tools: CAD software, simulation/FEA tools, MATLAB/Simulink for
modeling, and increasingly Python for data analysis and automation of
engineering workflows.
To grow: build a portfolio of real design projects (even personal/academic
ones) that show the full process from concept to analysis to iteration.
Learning to pair traditional mechanical design skills with basic
programming/scripting (e.

teration.
Learning to pair traditional mechanical design skills with basic
programming/scripting (e.g. automating repetitive analysis tasks) is
increasingly valuable and differentiates candidates in a competitive field.
Certifications like FE (Fundamentals of Engineering) and later PE
(Professional Engineer) matter more in some industries (civil-adjacent,
regulated industries) than others.

## Systems/Design Engineer
Systems and Design Engineers focus on how individual components fit into
a larger system - requirements definition, interface analysis, and
ensuring subsystems work together correctly (common in automotive,
aerospace, and complex product development).
Core skills: requirements engineering, systems thinking, cross-functional
communication (working with mechanical, electrical, a

ngineering, systems thinking, cross-functional
communication (working with mechanical, electrical, and software teams),
and documentation (architectural diagrams, requirement traceability).
To grow: experience working across multiple engineering disciplines
(not just one) is valuable here, since the role is fundamentally about
integration. Building experience with formal requirements/verification
processes (common in regulated industries like automotive or aerospace)
helps significantly for more senior systems engineering roles.

## Manufacturing/Process Engineer
Manufacturing Engineers design and improve the processes used to
produce products - focusing on efficiency, quality, and cost.
Core skills: process design and optimization, quality tools (Six Sigma,
DFMEA), understanding of manufa

e skills: process design and optimization, quality tools (Six Sigma,
DFMEA), understanding of manufacturing equipment/automation, and basic
statistics for process control.
To grow: a Six Sigma certification (Green Belt or higher) is highly
valued in this field and demonstrates structured process-improvement
skill. Hands-on plant floor experience, even early in a career, builds
credibility that's hard to get purely from classroom knowledge.

FINANCE - CAREER GUIDE

## Financial Analyst
Financial Analysts evaluate financial data to guide business decisions - things
like budgeting, forecasting, and investment analysis.
Core skills: strong Excel skills (financial modeling, pivot tables), understanding
of financial statements (income statement, balance sheet, cash flow), and
increasingly, basic knowledge of a BI tool (Power BI, Tableau) or SQL for
pulling data directly.
Common tools: Excel, financial modeling templates, ERP systems (SAP, Oracle),
and reporting/BI dashboards.
To grow: build strong Excel modeling skills first - this is the single most
requested skill for this role. Learning SQL and a BI tool sets you apart, since
many analysts still rely on manually exported spreadsheets. Certifications
like CFA (Chartered Financial

analysts still rely on manually exported spreadsheets. Certifications
like CFA (Chartered Financial Analyst) are valuable for more senior/investment
focused roles but are a long-term commitment, not needed for entry-level roles.

## Accountant
Accountants track and record an organization's financial transactions, ensure
compliance with regulations, and prepare financial statements and tax filings.
Core skills: bookkeeping fundamentals, understanding of GAAP/accounting
standards, attention to detail, and comfort with accounting software.
Common tools: QuickBooks, Tally, SAP, Excel, and tax preparation software.
To grow: a professional certification (CPA in the US, CA in India, or
equivalent) significantly increases career ceiling and salary. Early career,
focus on mastering one accounting

significantly increases career ceiling and salary. Early career,
focus on mastering one accounting software thoroughly and understanding the
full month-end/quarter-end close process, since that's core to almost every
accounting job.

## Investment Analyst
Investment Analysts research companies, markets, and securities to support
investment decisions, often within an investment bank, asset management firm,
or private equity fund.
Core skills: financial modeling and valuation (DCF, comparable company
analysis), strong understanding of markets, and the ability to write clear
investment research/recommendations.
Common tools: Excel (advanced modeling), Bloomberg Terminal, and increasingly
Python for quantitative analysis.
To grow: this is a competitive, often networking-driven field. Build a

n for quantitative analysis.
To grow: this is a competitive, often networking-driven field. Build a
portfolio of practice financial models, follow markets closely and be able
to discuss investment theses, and target internships early since this field
weighs relevant experience heavily.

HEALTHCARE - CAREER GUIDE

## Registered Nurse / Clinical Staff
Registered Nurses and other clinical staff provide direct patient care -
monitoring patients, administering treatments/medications, and coordinating
with doctors and other care team members.
Core skills: clinical knowledge relevant to the care setting, strong
attention to detail (medication accuracy, documentation), communication
with patients and families, and the ability to stay calm under pressure.
Common requirements: a nursing license (RN licensure, which requires
completing an accredited nursing program and passing a licensing exam),
and often certifications specific to a specialty (e.g. critical care,
pediatrics).
To grow: specializing in a high-demand clinical area (ICU, ER, surgical)
often increases both pay and oppor

: specializing in a high-demand clinical area (ICU, ER, surgical)
often increases both pay and opportunities. Pursuing further education
(e.g. Nurse Practitioner) opens up more autonomous clinical roles with
higher earning potential, though it requires additional schooling.

## Healthcare Administrator
Healthcare Administrators manage the business and operational side of
healthcare facilities - staffing, budgets, compliance, and coordinating
between clinical staff and organizational leadership.
Core skills: healthcare regulations/compliance knowledge (e.g. HIPAA),
budgeting and operations management, and the ability to communicate well
with both clinical staff and non-clinical leadership.
Common tools: healthcare management systems, scheduling software, and
standard budgeting/reporting too

mmon tools: healthcare management systems, scheduling software, and
standard budgeting/reporting tools.
To grow: a degree in Healthcare Administration or an MBA with a healthcare
focus helps for more senior roles. Building experience in a specific
functional area first (e.g. billing/compliance, then operations) is a
common path toward broader administrative leadership roles.

HUMAN RESOURCES - CAREER GUIDE

## HR Generalist
HR Generalists handle a broad mix of HR functions - onboarding, employee
relations, policy administration, benefits coordination, and often light
recruiting - especially in small-to-mid sized companies.
Core skills: strong communication, knowledge of basic labor law/compliance,
conflict resolution, and organizational skills to juggle many different
employee-facing tasks at once.
Common tools: HRIS systems (Workday, BambooHR, SAP SuccessFactors), payroll
software, and standard office tools.
To grow: HR Generalist is often a stepping stone toward either HR Management
(people leadership) or a specialized track (recruiting, compensation &
benefits, L&D). Building visible expertise in one area (e.g. becoming the
go-to person for onboarding or ben

, L&D). Building visible expertise in one area (e.g. becoming the
go-to person for onboarding or benefits) helps with a specialization move.
An HR certification (SHRM-CP or similar) helps credibility, especially for
those without a formal HR degree.

## Recruiter
Recruiters source, screen, and manage the hiring pipeline for open roles,
working closely with hiring managers to fill positions.
Core skills: sourcing techniques (LinkedIn, job boards, referrals), strong
interviewing/screening ability, negotiation (especially for offers), and
the ability to manage many candidates/roles simultaneously without dropping
the ball.
Common tools: Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) like Greenhouse or Lever,
LinkedIn Recruiter, and scheduling tools.
To grow: specializing (technical recruiting, executive se

LinkedIn Recruiter, and scheduling tools.
To grow: specializing (technical recruiting, executive search, campus
recruiting) often leads to higher pay and more interesting work than staying
generalist. Building a strong network and reputation for placing good
candidates matters more here than almost any certification.

## HR Manager
HR Managers oversee HR strategy and a team of HR staff, often owning
policy decisions, performance management systems, and being a key partner
to senior leadership on people matters.
Core skills: people leadership, strategic thinking (aligning HR practices
to business goals), deep knowledge of employment law/compliance, and
strong stakeholder management with leadership.
To grow: this role typically requires several years of HR Generalist or
specialist experienc

ership.
To grow: this role typically requires several years of HR Generalist or
specialist experience first. Building experience managing a team, leading
a policy or culture initiative, and developing comfort discussing HR
metrics/ROI with leadership all help make this transition.

INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY - CAREER GUIDE

## Software Engineer
Software Engineers design, build, and maintain software applications and systems.
Core skills: at least one programming language (Python, Java, C++, JavaScript),
data structures and algorithms, version control (Git), understanding of software
development lifecycle (SDLC), and familiarity with testing practices.
Common tools: Git/GitHub, an IDE (VS Code, IntelliJ), cloud platforms (AWS/Azure/GCP),
and increasingly, basic familiarity with CI/CD pipelines.
To grow: build small personal projects and put them on GitHub, contribute to open
source, learn one framework deeply (e.g. React for web, or a backend framework)
rather than many frameworks shallowly. For entry-level roles, focus on strong
fundamentals (data structures, algorithms)

meworks shallowly. For entry-level roles, focus on strong
fundamentals (data structures, algorithms) since many interviews test this directly.
To transition into this role from a non-software background (e.g. IT support,
systems administration): highlight any scripting/automation work you've already
done, take a structured course in one language, and build 2-3 small projects that
demonstrate you can write and ship working code.

## Systems Administrator
Systems Administrators manage an organization's servers, networks, and IT
infrastructure - keeping systems running, secure, and up to date.
Core skills: operating systems (Windows Server, Linux/Red Hat), Active Directory,
networking fundamentals, backup and disaster recovery, and security basics
(patching, firewalls, access control).
Common

als, backup and disaster recovery, and security basics
(patching, firewalls, access control).
Common tools: Active Directory, VMware/virtualization tools, monitoring tools
(Nagios, SolarWinds), scripting (PowerShell or Bash) for automating routine tasks.
To grow: learn scripting to automate repetitive admin tasks (this is a common
path from "hands-on admin" to "IT automation/DevOps"), pursue certifications
(CompTIA Server+, Microsoft certifications, RHCSA for Linux), and gain exposure
to cloud infrastructure since many companies are moving away from fully
on-premise setups.

## IT Support / Helpdesk
IT Support staff handle day-to-day technical issues for employees - password
resets, hardware troubleshooting, software installs, and basic network issues.
Core skills: patience and clear commu

troubleshooting, software installs, and basic network issues.
Core skills: patience and clear communication (you're explaining technical
things to non-technical people), basic troubleshooting methodology, ticketing
systems, and a working knowledge of common operating systems and office software.
To grow: this is often an entry point into IT. Moving toward Systems
Administration means picking up server management and networking; moving
toward Software Engineering means learning to code; moving toward
Cybersecurity means learning security fundamentals and pursuing a
certification like Security+.

MARKETING & DIGITAL MEDIA - CAREER GUIDE

## Marketing Coordinator / Manager
Marketing Coordinators and Managers plan and execute campaigns to promote
a company's products, services, or brand - across channels like social
media, email, content, and paid advertising.
Core skills: campaign planning, content creation/copywriting, basic
analytics (understanding what's working and why), and familiarity with
marketing platforms.
Common tools: social media platforms and schedulers (Hootsuite, Buffer),
email marketing tools (Mailchimp, HubSpot), Google Analytics, and design
tools (Canva, or Adobe Creative Suite for more design-heavy roles).
To grow: build a portfolio of real campaigns you've run, even small ones,
and be able to talk about actual results (engagement, leads generated,
growth numbers

en small ones,
and be able to talk about actual results (engagement, leads generated,
growth numbers) - this is a field where a portfolio matters more than
almost any other credential. Learning basic data analysis (Google
Analytics, or even just Excel) sets marketers apart, since so much of
modern marketing is data-informed.

## Digital Media Specialist
Digital Media Specialists focus specifically on digital channels - social
media, video content, website content, and online advertising - creating
and managing a brand's digital presence.
Core skills: content creation (video, graphics, or writing depending on
specialization), platform-specific knowledge (what works on Instagram vs
LinkedIn vs YouTube), and basic performance tracking.
Common tools: video/photo editing tools (Adobe Premiere,

YouTube), and basic performance tracking.
Common tools: video/photo editing tools (Adobe Premiere, Photoshop,
Canva), social media management platforms, and analytics dashboards for
each platform.
To grow: specializing in one content format (video editing, short-form
content, or a specific platform) and building a visible portfolio (a
personal Instagram/YouTube/portfolio site showing real work) is often
more valuable early on than a broad but shallow skill set. Staying
current with platform algorithm/format changes is a constant, ongoing
part of this career.

## Public Relations / Communications
PR and Communications professionals manage how an organization is
perceived publicly - media relations, press releases, crisis
communication, and often internal communications too.
Core skills: st

ations, press releases, crisis
communication, and often internal communications too.
Core skills: strong writing (press releases, statements, talking points),
relationship-building with media contacts, and calm, clear judgment
under pressure (especially for crisis communications).
To grow: building real media relationships and a portfolio of coverage
you've helped secure is the strongest signal in this field. Internships
at agencies or in-house PR teams are a common and valuable entry point,
since so much of the job depends on trust and existing relationships
that take time to build.

SALES - CAREER GUIDE

## Sales Representative
Sales Representatives (often called Sales Development Reps or Account
Executives depending on the stage of the sales cycle they own) generate
leads, pitch products/services, and close deals with customers.
Core skills: communication and persuasion, resilience (handling rejection),
active listening to understand customer needs, and basic pipeline/CRM
management.
Common tools: CRM software (Salesforce, HubSpot), email/outreach tools,
and increasingly LinkedIn Sales Navigator for prospecting.
To grow: track and be able to talk about your numbers (quota attainment,
deals closed, pipeline generated) since sales is one of the most metrics-
driven career paths. Moving from an entry Sales Development Rep role to a
full Account Executive role usually re

r paths. Moving from an entry Sales Development Rep role to a
full Account Executive role usually requires demonstrating strong lead
qualification and a track record of hitting targets.

## Account Executive
Account Executives own the full sales cycle for a set of accounts/prospects -
from qualifying interest through negotiating and closing the deal, and often
managing the ongoing client relationship afterward.
Core skills: consultative selling (understanding a client's business problem,
not just pitching features), negotiation, deal strategy, and relationship
management for renewals/upsells.
Common tools: CRM (Salesforce), proposal/quoting tools, and video conferencing
for demos.
To grow: build expertise in the specific industry/product you sell in - deep
domain knowledge (e.g. understand

uild expertise in the specific industry/product you sell in - deep
domain knowledge (e.g. understanding a client's business model) differentiates
top performers. Developing account planning skills and moving toward larger,
more strategic accounts is a common growth path toward Senior AE or Sales
Manager roles.
